101.question: In a For Loop, what happens by default with an output tunnel to which a scalar value generated on each iteration is connected?

options.a: Auto-indexing is enabled by default, so the tunnel accumulates the values into an array
options.b: Auto-indexing is disabled by default, so only the last value is kept
options.c: LabVIEW generates an error because tunnels do not support auto-indexing in For Loops
options.d: Auto-indexing is only possible if the value is Boolean

101.explanation: In a For Loop, auto-indexing on output tunnels is enabled by default: each value generated on an iteration is automatically appended to an output array.

102.question: In a While Loop, what happens by default with auto-indexing on output tunnels, in contrast to the For Loop?

options.a: Auto-indexing is disabled by default; the tunnel keeps only the last value generated unless it is enabled manually
options.b: Auto-indexing is enabled by default, just as in the For Loop
options.c: The While Loop does not allow output tunnels
options.d: The While Loop always requires Shift Registers in order to have outputs

102.explanation: Unlike the For Loop, in a While Loop auto-indexing on outputs is disabled by default (since the number of iterations is not known in advance); it can be enabled manually by right-clicking the tunnel.

103.question: A For Loop has the value 4 wired to its N terminal, and inside it generates scalar values connected to an output tunnel with auto-indexing enabled. How many elements will the resulting array outside the loop have?

options.a: 4 elements, one for each iteration executed
options.b: 1 element, the last one generated
options.c: 0 elements, because the loop cannot produce arrays
options.d: An indeterminate number, different on each run

103.explanation: With auto-indexing enabled on the output, the final array contains exactly one element per iteration executed; with N=4, the resulting array will have 4 elements.

104.question: Which type of array is shown in LabVIEW with two indexes inside the control's display (row and column)?

options.a: A two-dimensional (2D) array
options.b: A one-dimensional (1D) array
options.d: A multidimensional enum

104.explanation: A two-dimensional array is shown on the front panel with two index fields: one for the row and one for the column.

105.question: What is the fundamental restriction on the data types that can be stored inside a single array in LabVIEW?

options.a: All elements of the array must be of the same data type
options.b: Elements can be of any data type, freely mixed
options.c: Only numeric types are allowed inside an array
options.d: Only Booleans are allowed inside an array

105.explanation: Unlike a cluster, an array requires all of its elements to be homogeneous, that is, of exactly the same data type.

106.question: Which function finds the maximum and minimum value within a numeric array, along with their indexes?

options.a: Array Max & Min
options.b: Sort 1D Array
options.d: Search 1D Array

106.explanation: Array Max & Min scans the array and returns both the maximum and minimum values found, along with the position (index) where each one is located.

107.question: Which function finds the first position at which a given value appears within a one-dimensional array?

options.a: Search 1D Array
options.b: Array Max & Min
options.d: Index Array

107.explanation: Search 1D Array looks for a specific element within the array and returns the index of its first occurrence, or -1 if it is not found.

108.question: What happens if you use Index Array with an index greater than or equal to the size of the array (out of range)?

options.a: LabVIEW returns the default value of the array's data type, without generating a run-time error that stops the VI
options.b: LabVIEW immediately stops execution of the VI with a critical error
options.d: LabVIEW automatically clamps the index to the last valid value

108.explanation: Accessing an out-of-range index with Index Array does not generate a fatal run-time error; instead, LabVIEW returns the default value of the corresponding data type (for example, 0 for numerics).

109.question: Which of the following is a good reason to prefer an array over creating multiple individual controls/variables for similar data?

options.a: It allows a set of homogeneous data to be processed uniformly and scalably using loops and array functions
options.b: Arrays always use less memory than any individual variable, without exception
options.c: Arrays are mandatory in order to use SubVIs
options.d: An array cannot be traversed with a loop

109.explanation: Using an array makes it easier to process collections of data of the same type with loops and specialized functions (Build Array, Index Array, and so on), instead of duplicating code for each individual variable.

110.question: Which visual representation identifies an array control or indicator on the Front Panel?

options.a: A container with a numeric index on its left border and a template element inside
options.b: A container with colored tabs
options.d: A gray-background container with no borders

110.explanation: On the Front Panel, an array is shown as a container with an index box on the left and, inside it, the 'template' element that defines the data type of all the array's elements.

111.question: A 2-element array is connected to the input tunnel of a For Loop with auto-indexing enabled, and in addition the N terminal is wired with the value 5. What happens when the loop runs?

options.a: The loop executes only 2 iterations, since LabVIEW uses the smaller of N and the size of the auto-indexed array
options.b: The loop executes 5 iterations, generating an error when it tries to read the non-existent third element
options.c: The loop executes 7 iterations, adding both values together
options.d: The VI cannot compile in this scenario

111.explanation: When there is a conflict between N and the size of an auto-indexed array, LabVIEW always honours the smaller of the two values to avoid out-of-range access.

112.question: Which function is used to remove one or more elements from an array starting at a given index?

options.a: Delete From Array
options.b: Replace Array Subset
options.d: Array Subset

112.explanation: Delete From Array removes one or more elements from an array starting at the given position, returning the resulting array without those elements.

113.question: Which function is used to insert one or more elements into an existing array at a specific position?

options.a: Insert Into Array
options.b: Build Array
options.d: Index Array

113.explanation: Insert Into Array adds one or more new elements into an existing array, at the given position, shifting the following elements.

114.question: Which of the following options correctly describes an empty array in LabVIEW?

options.a: A valid array that exists but has zero elements (size 0)
options.b: A data type error
options.c: An array that can only contain Booleans
options.d: An array that necessarily contains one element with a NULL value

114.explanation: An empty array is perfectly valid in LabVIEW: it is an array whose size (Array Size) is 0, with no elements, but which retains its base data type.

115.question: Which function sorts the elements of a one-dimensional array from lowest to highest?

options.a: Sort 1D Array
options.b: Search 1D Array
options.d: Reverse 1D Array

115.explanation: Sort 1D Array reorders the elements of the input array in ascending order, returning a new sorted array.

116.question: When you resize an array indicator on the Front Panel to show more than one element, what is being modified?

options.a: Only the view/display of the array, not its actual contents or its logical size
options.b: The actual logical size of the array, adding new empty elements
options.d: The order of the array's elements

116.explanation: Enlarging an array indicator on the front panel only changes how many elements are visible at once; it does not alter the actual contents or the logical size of the array in memory.

117.question: You have a 2D array of 3 rows by 4 columns. When you apply the Array Size function to this array, what does the function return?

options.a: A two-element array: {3, 4}, representing the number of rows and columns
options.b: A single integer: 12, the total number of elements
options.d: An error, because Array Size does not accept 2D arrays

117.explanation: For multidimensional arrays, Array Size returns a 1D array where each element gives the size of one dimension (in this case, 3 rows and 4 columns).

118.question: What happens if an empty array (0 elements) is connected to the input tunnel of a For Loop with auto-indexing enabled, and no other value is wired to N?

options.a: The loop executes no iterations
options.b: The loop executes exactly one iteration with a default value
options.d: The VI breaks at compile time

118.explanation: When auto-indexing determines the iteration count from an empty array, the For Loop executes zero iterations, since there are no elements to index.

119.question: Which of the following functions does NOT typically belong to the Array functions palette in LabVIEW?

options.a: Bundle by Name
options.b: Build Array
options.d: Array Size

119.explanation: Bundle by Name belongs to the Cluster palette, not the Array palette; it is used to write cluster elements by name, not to manipulate arrays.

120.question: On a block diagram, what visually distinguishes a wire carrying an array from a wire carrying a scalar value of the same base type?

options.a: The array wire is drawn thicker (a heavier line) than the scalar one
options.b: The array wire is always black
options.c: The array wire flashes during execution
options.d: There is no visual difference between the two

120.explanation: LabVIEW increases the line thickness of wires carrying arrays compared with those carrying an equivalent scalar value, helping to visually identify the kind of data structure.

121.question: What is a cluster in LabVIEW?

options.a: A data structure that groups one or more elements of potentially different data types into a single terminal
options.b: A collection of elements that must all be of the same data type
options.d: A specialized type of loop

121.explanation: Unlike an array, a cluster can group elements of different data types (for example, a numeric together with a string and a Boolean) into a single unit of data.

122.question: What is the main difference between an array and a cluster with regard to the data types they can contain?

options.a: The array requires all of its elements to be of the same type, whereas the cluster accepts elements of different types
options.b: The cluster requires all of its elements to be of the same type, whereas the array accepts different types
options.c: Both require exactly the same data type in all of their elements
options.d: Neither of the two allows data types to be mixed

122.explanation: Arrays are homogeneous (the same type in all elements), whereas clusters are heterogeneous and can combine, for example, a numeric, a string and a Boolean.

123.question: Which property of the elements inside a cluster is essential for the Bundle and Unbundle functions (the unnamed ones)?

options.a: The order in which they were added to the cluster
options.b: The background color of the cluster
options.c: The name of the cluster itself
options.d: The amount of RAM available

123.explanation: The order of the elements within the cluster determines the position at which Bundle and Unbundle (positional) read or write each value; changing that order can break existing code.

124.question: Which function is used to create a cluster from individual elements, or to modify one or more elements of an existing cluster by position?

options.a: Bundle
options.b: Unbundle
options.d: Index Array

124.explanation: Bundle assembles a new cluster from individual values, or modifies elements of an existing cluster wired to its input, referencing them by position.

125.question: Which function is used to extract all the individual elements of a cluster, in the order in which they were defined?

options.a: Unbundle
options.b: Bundle
options.d: Index Array

125.explanation: Unbundle breaks a cluster into its individual elements, exposing each one as a separate output, in the cluster's positional order.
